📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • on Friday when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session.
  • It has been revealed that following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget.
  • Sources indicate that reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It was 5:55 a.m. on Friday when the Bundestag's Budget Committee concluded its final session.

It has been revealed that following nearly 16 hours of negotiations, lawmakers from the conservative Christian Democratic Union(CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties, along with their coalition partners from the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), voted in favor of the 2027 draft budget. The opposition parties — the environmentalist Greens, the socialist Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) — voted against it. With that, the way is now clear for the final vote in the Bundestag on November 27.

Sources indicate that reading through the nearly 1,000-page document requires a great deal of number-crunching. Next year, the federal government prepares to spend around €561 billion ($620 billion).

According to recent reports, but here's the problem: it won't collect nearly enough revenue to cover these expenses. With a shortfall of €123 billion, borrowing will be needed to bridge the gap.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, but that's not the only problem. On top of all this debt, Germany also has loans for defense spending and for the renovation of the dilapidated infrastructure. Approved by the Bundestag in 2025, these special funds are set to be in place for multiple years.

If the newly introduced debt for 2027 is factored in, the total borrowing amounts to over €210 billion. This is the second-highest level of borrowing in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany. The only time Germany borrowed more was during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021, when borrowing reached €215.4 billion.

Industry observers note that this development has drawn sharp criticism from opposition parties. Green Party lawmaker Sebastian Schäfer and his colleague Dietmar Bartsch of the Left Party called it a "gigantic mountain of debt," an "untrustworthy" budget, "irresponsible" policies at the expense of future generations and a lack of future prospects.

Industry observers note that to understand the reasons behind the growing debt, one has to look beyond the numbers. Every federal budget is a snapshot of the priorities set by a government and a country — in terms of the economy, social complications, security and geopolitics.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

For 2027, that story continues to be one of crises and wars. While Russia's war against Ukraine is driving up defense spending, the faltering economy is also demanding latest investments. At the same time, Germany's population is aging rapidly, which is driving up social spending.

In a recent development, what's more, the crumbling infrastructure must be repaired and modernized, and the energy transition is costing billions. And more than half of all this debt is going toward security and defense.

Russia's war against Ukraine will enter its sixth year in 2027. As of the end of June, the federal government estimated its overall support for Ukraine to have reached approximately €100 billion. In response to a request from the AfD in the Bundestag, the government stated: "The federal government will continue to provide Ukraine with political, financial, humanitarian, civil and military support for as long as necessary.".

Recent findings suggest that the rearmament of the Bundeswehr and spending on NATO are also putting massive pressure on the budget. The defense budget is set to grow to just under €110 billion in 2027, an increase of around €27 billion compared to last year. Added to this are expenditures from the Bundeswehr's special fund.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, by far the largest single budget item comes from the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is set to grow to over €200 billion. There are looks for cost-cutting measures, for example, in basic income support for job seekers. But the costs of old-age pension benefits continue to rise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

People born in the 1960s have begun to retire. Back then, more than 1 million children were born each year. But birth rates nearly halved in the early 1970s and have continued to decline since then. As a result, there will be an increasing number of retirees and a decreasing number of working-age individuals in the coming years.

Recent findings suggest that the pension funds cannot be financed by the pension contributions of this dwindling workforce and have to be subsidized by the government. Already, contributions to the pension insurance system — which are split equally between employees and employers — will have to be increased. They are expected to rise to just under 20% of gross salary.

It has been revealed that the Federal Employment Agency, too, has long been unable to make ends meet on contributions alone. In 2027, subsidies of more than €8 billion from the federal budget are planned.

Anyone comparing Germany's current budget situation with that of past years will be rubbing their eyes in disbelief. It wasn't that long ago that Germany was considered a model of fiscal discipline. Between 2014 and 2019, the federal budget managed to avoid taking on new debt for six consecutive years. In some years, there was even money left over.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

But the era of "balanced budgets" came to an abrupt end with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. However, today Germany is still enjoying the benefits of those years of fiscal stability. Compared to other countries, Germany is still in relatively good shape.

The key indicator is not the amount of debt along but the debt-to-GDP ratio. It indicates how high the national debt is in relation to annual economic output.

According to recent reports, at the end of 2025, it stood at 63.5% for Germany. France, on the other hand, stands at over 110% and Italy at about 135% to 140%, while the US is well above 100%. However, in its latest fall report, the German Council of Economic Experts warned that Germany could be heading down a dangerous path. If debt continues to rise at this rate, the debt-to-GDP ratio could climb to 100% by 2040.

Sources indicate that this would also put Germany's creditworthiness on the financial markets at risk. Germany is the only country among the seven leading democratic industrialized nations (G7) that still holds a triple-A (AAA) rating. This is the highest possible credit rating on the financial markets. It signals to investors that the risk of default on German government bonds is extremely low.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

This also means that interest rates on new loans are not set as high. This is an vital point, as interest payments place an increasing burden on the federal budget each year. By 2027, approximately €42 billion in interest payments are expected to be due.

According to recent reports, at the end of November, the Bundestag will hold its final debate on the draft budget. Should changes be expected by then? There is disagreement within the government over whether a reduction in the electricity tax might still be possible.

The prospect of such a reduction had been raised by Chancellor Friedrich Merz. On Friday, during a European leaders summit in Dublin, he reiterated: "I expect that we will discuss this again next Tuesday in the coalition committee, and I remain committed to my goal of lowering the electricity tax to the European minimum — in full — starting next year.".

Manchester United are looking for a first January signing that could ruffle a few feathers across the Premier League.

The Red Devils have just appointed Mauricio Pochettino as manager, with the Argentine taking over a squad devoid of much confidence and languishing 18th in the Premier League table.

Attention has already turned to the winter transfer window, however, as Manchester United look to repeat a trick that worked for them last summer.

Last summer, United beat Arsenal to the signing of Benjamin Sesko when they met RB Leipzig's valuation of the Slovenian at a time when the Gunners refused to.

Sesko has been a solid addition at Old Trafford, while the champions opted to sign Viktor Gyokeres instead, with the Swedish hitman blowing hot and cold in the Premier League.

With Arsenal now in for Antonio Nusa, transfer insider Gianluca Di Marzio has told Wettfreunde.net United have interest in the Norwegian – and a major advantage.

“Roma wanted Antonio Nusa during the summer, but he decided to stay,” the Italian journalist remarked, adding, “Manchester City like him a lot, Manchester United like him a lot as well.”.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

With United needing to reinforce in attacking areas – having lost Sesko to injury until the New Year – Di Marzio notes that Arsenal aren't likely to make a move in January and would rather wait until the summer.

FourFourTwo understands that Leipzig are under no pressure to sell the star after the nine-figure sale of Yan Diomande to Real Madrid over the summer – so should United present an extraordinary offer to the player and to Leipzig, as they did with Sesko, they may well be able to land him ahead of the Gunners.

“He will be around €70 or €80 million,” Di Marzio added, “but it’s much more likely that he can leave in the summer.”.

After a solid World Cup 2026 with Norway over the summer, Nusa has started the campaign on fire for Leipzig, notching 11 goals and assists in his first nine Bundesliga fixtures and scoring against Manchester City in the Champions League.

The 21-year-old agreed a £25m deal to Brentford in 2024, only for the move to collapse at the last minute.

Nusa is worth €45m, according to Transfermarkt. Manchester United travel to Liverpool when Premier League action resumes this weekend.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By KATE MCGREAVY, EXECUTIVE SPORTS EDITOR.

Published: 04:01 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 05:10 EST, 22 November 2026.

Bruno Fernandes has revealed there are no ongoing contract negotiations with Manchester United after he rejected their proposed new deal.

The Manchester United captain's contract is set to expire in June 2027, which means that if the club and player fail to agree fresh terms, Fernandes will be free to discuss a summer move with clubs abroad as early as the January transfer window.

Fernandes has divided United fans during their dire season so far but fresh manager Mauricio Pochettino confirmed he will remain as captain in his first press conference on Friday.

It was widely known that discussions between Fernandes and Man United began over the summer, on the heels of a strong campaign which saw him named Men's PFA Player of the Year.

But Fernandes has now shed light on his future by admitting contract talks have stalled after the club put a deal on the table.

'No, there's no negotiations ongoing,' Fernandes told Sky Sports ahead of United's trip to Anfield this afternoon. 'But I've seen people saying that he's asked for more money, he's asked for more years. If I wanted more money I wouldn't be here.

Bruno Fernandes has revealed there are no ongoing contract negotiations with Man United.

In a recent development, 'I had somewhere to go to get much more money than being at Manchester United. I could have been in a place that is much warmer than Manchester. Two summers ago, three summers ago, last summer, I always had a chance to leave and I always chose to be here.

'The thing is I've always showed how much I care about the club and how much I want to win at this club.

'And I've always said the moment the club thinks is the time for me to move on, I will move on. I'm not going to be the player that I've seen many in this time at Man United they're going to stay here just by staying, just by finishing my contract and then we will see.

'In the moment the club says "Bruno, it's time to part ways", I'm going to be the first one walking out the door.

'Yeah the club offered me a new contract so I think that from their side indicates that they want me to stay.

Sources indicate that 'As I said there are no negotiations going on. We spoke about the contract at the end of last season. We came in the beginning of the season speaking about the contract but about the context of the team and the club I just put that to a side because I don't think it's the right moment, neither for me, neither for the club to be talking about negotiations because the most important thing now is that the club gets back to winning games.'.

The club may yet seek to trigger the 12-month extension in Fernandes' contract. Daily Mail Sport understands Galatasaray as well as AC Milan and Saudi are among those monitoring developments.

The Portuguese was linked with a significant-money move to Saudi Arabia last year with Al-Hilal reportedly willing to offer a contract worth up to £200m to the midfielder, on top of a £100m transfer fee to United, but he chose to commit his future to the Red Devils.

United presently sit in the relegation zone after a 40-year worst-ever start to the season. Fernandes publicly questioned the former manager's tactics after his side's Champions League thrashing at the hands of Como, and has struggled to find form this season.

Fernandes was brought back into the fold after going through a brief period of being frozen out of Michael Carrick's squad following his incendiary comments following defeat in Italy last month.

Fernandes, who is usually very deliberate in what he states in the media, was scathing in his criticism of coaches after the Como debacle.

'It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave a little space in behind and try to get the ball in the first moment, to wait for them, to give them the ball,' he noted.

'But sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confident, they have so many bodies behind the ball that make you run a lot, make people get frustrated, and then obviously when you recover the ball the legs are, and the brain, much more difficult to make it work.'.

In a recent development, his post-Como interview was widely condemned by fans and pundits alike, with Gary Neville lamenting: 'If that's your captain saying that, imagine what they're saying in the dressing room behind closed doors when no one's listening. That's horrific.'.

He also told Fernandes to 'read the room' and accused him of being an 'excuse merchant' on his podcast.

Fernandes was left on the bench for Man United's next Premier League appointment, a loss to Bournemouth, before returning to the starting XI against Chelsea the following matchday.

After Man United's comeback win against Roma, Fernandes was defiant in his post-match remarks as he stressed that he had not been sanctioned for undermining Carrick with his initial interview.

'The club needed that win. The players needed that win. It is something we needed as a group of players and staff,' he stated. 'We have been working so hard to get out of this situation together. It has been tough. There has been a lot of speculation in the media.

Mauricio Pochettino confirmed Fernandes will remain as captain in his first press conference.

It has been revealed that 'A lot of lies around many things that have happened at this club, between me and the manager, like that we have cleared the air. Nothing like that happened.

Sources indicate that 'The manager took a decision of making myself on the bench because I wasn't performing. And that's fair.

Industry observers note that 'Everyone felt like that was a punishment for the words that I had [after Como]. And if it was, it was right.

Recent findings suggest that 'The manager makes the decisions. I have to accept it. I have to go forward with that. It doesn't change the belief I have in the manager, the staff and every player at this club.

'And it doesn't change my aim to win every f***ing game that I have ahead of me.'.

Fernandes' comments were ultimately unable to keep Carrick in his job however, with the former club captain finally sacked on November 11 after an agonising three-day wait.

Man United's hierarchy, notably chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, have come under fire from the fanbase and within the club for their treatment of the departing coach, with Carrick taking two days of training at Carrington as they mulled his sacking.

Wilcox and Berrada jetted to Monaco to meet with Ineos chief Sir Jim Ratcliffe and discuss the departure of Carrick, with the club's Glazer ownership ratifying the decision to replace him with United States national team coach Pochettino.

Pochettino swapped the USA for United on Wednesday and will take charge of his first match against bitter rivals Liverpool today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although the millions of gamers who are pulling sickies would beg to differ, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI wasn’t the most exciting midnight launch involving a sprawling enterprise full of shady characters. Over in Zurich, the clock also struck 12 on the candidate deadline for next year’s Fifa presidential election, leaving those of us who have no interest in video games with our own chaotic, multi-billion-dollar sandbox where untouchable bosses bend the rules to suit themselves. While online carjackers are busy exploring a “most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world”, football’s real-life power brokers are gearing up for a March showdown in the actual city of Rabat.

For years, Gianni Infantino has looked nailed-on to glide into a fourth term of office completely unopposed, but following his disastrous Fifa Forward Enterprise wheeze to flog stakes in the World Cup to his American pals on the cheap, many of the emperor’s former allies have finally turned against him. In the wake of the revolt, European national associations withdrew their backing for Infantino and, on Thursday morning, Fifa confirmed the 56-year-old will face his first contested election since parking his backside on the throne a decade ago. Sadly for all those who would like nothing more than to see him deposed, Infantino remains the red-hot favourite in what will be a three-horse race.

In a recent development, leading the charge for the mutineers is Philippe Diallo, the 63-year-old French Football Federation president who was unanimously anointed as Europe’s preferred candidate after their actual preferred candidate, Arsène Wenger, decided not to throw his chapeau in the ring. His billing by Uefa’s vice-president, Laura McAllister, as a man “who can instigate real, meaningful and lasting reform” at Fifa conveniently overlooks the fact that, as recently as five months ago, Diallo’s own federation signed a letter formally endorsing Infantino again. Joining Diallo in the battle to prise Gianni’s fingers off the levers of power is Kozo Tashima, the 68-year-old honorary president of the Japan FA. He could yet stand aside to avoid a split of the vote from Fifa’s 211 members who want Infantino booted to the door marked “Do One!”. Unfortunately, Ramon Vega, the former Switzerland and Tottenham defender, won’t be on the ballot. He had again declared his candidacy but proved unable to scare up the five member-association endorsements required.

According to recent reports, between now and Fifa’s March congress, all three candidates must pass a Fifa eligibility and integrity check, a feat which shouldn’t be beyond the two pretenders, given Infantino has repeatedly come through it with flying colours while helping to overhaul the committees tasked with marking his papers along the way. Assuming he once again clears the hurdle of being vetted by his own organisation, the next four months promise a familiar blur of private jets, palm-greasing and disingenuous crawling. While a generation of gamers will spend winter pulling off virtual heists in Vice City, when it comes to bending the rules in your favour, nobody plays the game quite like the Fifa final boss.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Harry Kane is England’s newly introduced leading appearance-maker after passing Peter Shilton’s record last week – and he hasn’t been the only player tipped to reach the milestone over the years.

Shilton’s record of 125 Three Lions caps had stood since he made his final appearance for his country at the 1990 World Cup, before Kane played his 126th cap against Croatia, then made it 127 against Spain on Sunday.

Wayne Rooney had previously finished agonisingly short on 120, with David Beckham winning 115 caps, Steven Gerrard reaching 114, Ashley Cole making it to 107 and Frank Lampard clocking up 106.

Another player who looked on course to surpass Shilton at one point was Michael Owen, who won his 89th cap at the age of just 28, but didn’t add to his tally as injuries derailed his career.

Asked whether he feels he would have made it to 126 if the injuries hadn’t hit, the former striker is philosophical about it.

“I’m not that bothered about that, I had my time,” he told FFT. “In little moments when you think back over your career, you think of things, but that’s across the board, isn’t it?

“If I didn’t get injured then, would I have won more Golden Boots? Would I have won the Ballon d’Or more? Would I have won more of anything? You just never know. It’s one of those things.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“There’s no question about it, if I had Harry Kane’s constitution, there’s no doubt I would have scored many, many, many more goals than I did, played many, many, many more games than I did, and all the rest of it.

“But I’m happy with my lot, I played 89 times for England – that’s quite a lot. That’s just life, isn’t it? You can’t spend your life thinking ‘What if?’”.

Owen reserved praise for Kane, who has scored an incredible 93 goals during his 127 caps.

It has been revealed that “What he’s done is extraordinary really,” Owen remarked, speaking in association with soccer betting odds. “He’s fine-tuned his game to become one of the most lethal players on the planet. It’s strange because he’s not the fastest, he’s not got a trick that always beats a defender, it’s pure efficiency.

“His finishing is just lethal. I think he’s the best finisher on the planet by some way, whether it’s left foot, heading, placing the ball, power, his penalties are brilliant. He’s practised and practised all his life to become so elite.

“You need so many things when you’re a player. A lot of it comes naturally, but you need to hone your skills as well. Harry has been one of the most hard-working players of this generation and deserves everything he gets.”.

Breaking: European football body’s blueprint to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome.
  • It has been revealed that it will be one of the most eagerly devoured documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed.
  • The study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome.

It has been revealed that it will be one of the most eagerly devoured documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed. In September, the increasingly powerful European Football Clubs body unveiled a “feasibility study” into how it can become established on a more global scale, morphing into an organisation that represents clubs all over the world.

The study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future. It has the potential to transform a landscape destabilised by the scandals surrounding Fifa and Gianni Infantino.

Once considered a lobby group representing clubs’ interests in the face of domineering governing bodies, EFC has mushroomed into a behemoth with almost 1,000 members that has the potential to supplant those bodies.

Recent findings suggest that “Now is the time to create World Football Clubs,” the EFC chair, Nasser Al-Khelaïfi, told delegates at its general assembly in Copenhagen seven weeks ago. The desire to expand exists in plain sight and is perfectly natural, some with a close interest in the process point out, given players and domestic leagues already have their own global representative bodies.

However, others warn of “a takeover by stealth” and fear it is merely a fig leaf for the tightening of the top European clubs’ influence over the game’s shape.

Sources familiar with EFC’s intentions say it is examining how to enter the international football market as a competition organiser, floating the idea of organising more effective tournaments in different formats. That is the role of Fifa or continental organisations such as Uefa and Concacaf but, should leading clubs find a way to forge events of their own, they could reap financial and commercial benefits far beyond those on offer through the confederations.

In a recent development, the prospect has some of the established powers on high alert. “You’re starting to see one of the major unspoken faultlines in football open up,” one source says of EFC’s relationship with Uefa, which has become structurally closer in recent years, but is still conducted with an air of high mutual caution. “Friends close, enemies closer” is one characterisation of that relationship.

This particularly appears the case now that, in the wreckage of Infantino’s doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, all parties find themselves jostling for leverage. Beyond a dramatic increase in funding for the member associations, many senior figures in football have remarked that the biggest long-term consequence of FFE’s failure will be to increase the power of the biggest European clubs.

While the former development is already in motion, with Fifa announcing last month that it will hand over an additional $2.7bn (£2.05bn) from its reserves over the next four years, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn, the latter will not be far behind.

That is because EFC’s study is not alone in harbouring huge implications for football’s shape. As revealed in September, a joint venture between EFC and Fifa to run the commercial side of global club competitions like the Club World Cup has been in the works for some time, with the fallout from FFE emerging as the catalyst required to push it through.

Multiple sources say the joint venture, similar to the agreement under which Uefa and EFC have operated European club competitions since 2008 that was formalised last year with the creation of commercial entity UC3, is ready to proceed pending approval from Infantino.

One source with knowledge of the discussions claims Infantino had been holding up the deal until the FFE scandal broke in July, since when negotiations have accelerated. An announcement could be made at next month’s Fifa council meeting in Doha, although waiting until after March’s presidential election at the global governing body seems more likely.

The joint venture’s contents have caused particular concern within Uefa, whose hierarchy are believed to have made clear their wish that a deal between EFC and Fifa is not rushed through.

While Uefa have continued to attack Infantino forcibly and are on the verge of backing a candidate to stand against him in next year’s election, EFC has been largely silent since its chief executive, Charlie Marshall, sent an explosive letter to Fifa’s secretary general, Mattias Grafström, on 31 July.

Recent findings suggest that EFC strongly condemned FFE, with the Guardian revealing the body threatened to boycott future Club World Cups (CWC) and withdraw its endorsement of the international match calendar. The sell-off proposal was formally dropped the following day.

One particularly incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”.

In a recent development, al-Khelaïfi, who is also the president of Paris Saint-Germain, did not directly address the glitch during his speech in Copenhagen two months later and there are suggestions a mutually beneficial solution has been reached. The crisis may have landed EFC the terms they wanted.

“It’s not a matter of whether Gianni wins [the election], but what his mandate is, and who is behind it,” a senior source in European football said. “A large part of the answer is EFC. EFC is going to take over Fifa in the same way [it] took over Uefa. The substantial clubs have gained yet more power and control.

“EFC initially came out very hard against Gianni, but were quick to row back. They’ve been silent on the presidential election and other governance issues, as it’s clear they’ve reached an agreement with Fifa. The joint venture is the price of their silence.”.

The result is likely to be an acceleration of trends already under way. The biggest European clubs look set to make even more money from latest tournaments, particularly given they are likely to increase in size and regularity, beginning with a 48-team men’s Club World Cup in 2029.

Recent findings suggest that chelsea earned $115m (£85m) from winning the inaugural expanded tournament last year, with six European clubs in the top seven of the prize money table and Brazil’s Fluminense the only non-European side to earn more than $50m. Solidarity payments are also skewed towards Europe, whose clubs will receive 50% of the $250m pot despite providing only 12 of the 32 contestants. Those defending the status quo note that Europe generates about 70% of Fifa’s revenue.

Recent findings suggest that A senior source at another confederation stated the inevitable result of the joint venture would be less money for the rest of the world, certainly in proportional terms. “The most significant long-term result of the Fifa crisis will be to entrench the economic might of the biggest European clubs,” they said. “That means reduced access to competitions, less revenue and broadcast rights for the rest of us.

“The European clubs are well organised, economically rational and have taken advantage of the opportunity to extract something from Fifa. Gianni Infantino is in the business of writing cheques and will now be writing significant ones to clubs as well as member associations.”.

These developments are, at least, easily foreseeable. It is less straightforward to analyse how football’s face will change if a putative World Football Clubs gains the power many believe lies in its sights. “Every club around the world deserves to be represented; to have a voice, and a better chance to succeed,” Al-Khelaïfi mentioned in his September address. But the world’s wealthiest clubs stand poised to benefit from football’s crisis more handsomely than anyone.

Are Liverpool prepared for Grand Theft Auto to ruin their weekend preparation?

Ah s***, here we go again: GTA VI dropped this week to rapturous acclaim from critics and public alike, with the long-awaited video game responsible for plenty of us turning up to work a little bleary-eyed after an all-nighter in Vice City.

And given that Premier League footballers are often avid gamers – they have a lot of time on their hands – FPL players are going to have to take into account those last-minute “groin strains” that see major-hitters pull out of this weekend's action….

According to recent reports, in September 2013, Liverpool defender Daniel Agger suffered a freak abdominal injury when he overstretched to prevent a dumbbell from falling on his foot in training. Or did he?

No, he probably did: but while the story certainly made sense – and Agger even aggravated the injury after playing through the pain barrier – the fact that Grand Theft Auto V was released that week certainly led some to wonder whether the Dane had in fact pulled a sickie.

Agger was far from the only suspicious absentee that week in the league either, with high-profile names missing up and down the country.

Robin van Persie and David Silva both missed the Manchester derby, completely unexpectedly, with the stars ruled out late with sudden muscle injuries: Manchester United boss David Moyes even revealed that he'd given RVP the chance to play right up until that Sunday morning.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Theo Walcott was even named in Arsenal's starting line-up for Stoke City that weekend, but pulled out with a mysterious “abdominal problem”, paving the way for Serge Gnabry to step in, while Gareth Bale was expected to make his Real Madrid debut that weekend, only for a “thigh tweak” in the warm-up to rule him out.

Silva and Walcott both missed the following fixtures – suggesting they really did have an alibi, with the latter requiring surgery – though Van Persie and Bale both recovered to make the bench the following week (convenient).

Regardless, there will be plenty of speculation this time around when line-ups are confirmed as to who's really injured and who's spent all week on the console and not in a fit state for high-level football.

Premier League action resumes this weekend with all 20 teams in action.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 05:59 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 09:37 EST, 22 November 2026.
  • Argentina star Leandro Paredes collapsed during a live interview immediately after winning a trophy with his Boca Juniors side.
  • The 32-year-old was one of the focal points of a World Cup side that reached the final last summer, and went on to win the Copa Sudamericana on Saturday evening after beating Brazil's Atletico Mineiro 2-0 in Barranquilla.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By TAMARA PRENN, SENIOR SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 05:59 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 09:37 EST, 22 November 2026.

Argentina star Leandro Paredes collapsed during a live interview immediately after winning a trophy with his Boca Juniors side.

The 32-year-old was one of the focal points of a World Cup side that reached the final last summer, and went on to win the Copa Sudamericana on Saturday evening after beating Brazil's Atletico Mineiro 2-0 in Barranquilla.

But amid the thick humidity and Colombian heat, Paredes became overwhelmed moments after lifting the trophy.

After giving a brief interview, Paredes was captured closing his eyes, before falling towards the interviewer, who attempted to break his fall.

Instead, the former Paris Saint-Germain midfielder hit the ground, with attendants rushing to help him after his collapse.

Paredes had been taken off in the second-half after suffering from heat-related dizziness, with humidity at 80 per cent heading into the match, and 32-degree-temperatures.

Leandro Parades collapsed to the floor during a post-match interview after winning the Copa Sudamericana with Boca Juniors.

The interviewer attempted to break his fall as the former PSG crumpled to the turf.

'He felt dizzy towards the end of the first-half,' his manager Rodolfo Arruabarrena explained of the substitution. 'He improved a little during the break, but after 10 minutes in the second-half, you could see he was struggling.'.

Fortunately, Paredes was revived rapidly and treated in the treatment room, before re-joining his team's celebrations after claiming the South American trophy.

The star shared a brief statement on social media confirming he was fine after the interview aired.

'We're fine,' Paredes confirmed with a picture taken during treatment, before adding in a separate caption: 'Thanks to everyone for the messages, it was just a dizziness from so many turns together'.

Paredes' triumph for his club side comes months after agonising defeat to Spain in Upcoming York at the World Cup final in July.

Argentina were felled by a solitary goal from Ferran Torres to end their reign as world champions, before the match descended into petty scraps - with Paredes at the heart of the bad behaviour.

Paredes furiously shoved Spain substitute Gavi to the floor after the final whistle blew, earning himself a punchy 10-match suspension from FIFA.

He faced three assault charges, while teammate Nahuel Molina faced two, and both players were also fined $90,000 (£66,000).

Paredes himself admitted that the length of the ban had put his international future under consideration.

Recent findings suggest that 'It's going to be difficult for me to stay with the national team,' Paredes told the media in September. 'Because of the suspension as well, because of (Lionel Messi) Leo's decision. It's going to be difficult for everything to carry on as before.

'I haven't discussed it with the coach (Lionel Scaloni) yet, but we'll talk about it and see what decision I make.'.

Paredes' announcement came just days after Messi decided to hang up his international boots, with the talismanic Argentina superstar treated to a magnificent send-off during the early Autumn international break.

'Leo's legacy will live on forever because of what he achieved, for never giving up and for showing that dreams are hard-won, pursued and, in the end, fulfilled,' Paredes added.

Paredes updated fans after the incident to confirm he was okay before rejoining the festivities with his team-mates (Source: Instagram/Leandro Parades).

'We'd spoken in the final days of the World Cup about how the final would surely be his last match, but even so, we weren't prepared for that because of what he means to us.'.

Although unable to compete alongside him in their country's colours for one last time, Paredes joined Messi on the pitch in Buenos Aires for his final farewell, and shared an emotional tribute post to his former captain.

'THANK YOU FOR ABSOLUTELY EVERYTHING CAPTAIN,' he captioned a carousel of photos of himself and Messi.

'It was a dream to be able to have achieved everything we achieved together and to have defended this shirt and our country with you, I'm leaving and we'll miss you always.

'It was a pleasure to be one of your soldiers for all these years and I will be forever! I love you buddy.'.

Reliving the drama: England and Argentina stars watch 1986 classic with fresh eyes

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (825 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Is there anything latest to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina.
  • The rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation.

Recent findings suggest that “Is there anything latest to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. Flora told an audience at the London film festival premiere of the film that she played her best card then and showed Lineker an image of Maradona with Queen in 1981, during the band’s tour of Argentina. Maradona wearing a union jack T-shirt and Freddie Mercury an Argentina strip. It worked. Lineker noted yes.

The rock’n’roll angle, with Brian May as a talking head, is one of the very few details the film-makers added to Andrés Burgo’s book, The Match, on which the documentary is based. The directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco play with the timeline, hopping between past and present across 91 minutes, the exact duration of the match itself. Anecdotes that now form part of Argentina’s football folklore are spliced with excellent archive material.

In a recent development, “There are two types of humans,” Jorge Valdano narrates, “Carlos Bilardo and everyone else.” Ricardo “El Gringo” Giusti recounts how he buried a sweet in the pitch before kick-off of every game, just one of the many cábalas the Argentina squad religiously followed under pressure from their obsessive manager. On the eve of the match with England, the players requested lighter shirts as the official ones were too heavy when drenched in sweat. Footage of women working at the squad hotel hand-stitching the numbers on to light T-shirts bought locally, shot by the players themselves with a handheld camera, conveys an intimacy in stark contrast to grainy archive material depicting British explorers in the South Atlantic.

Rather than run-of-the-mill talking head-style interviews with members of both teams, the interviewees are shot in monochrome, widescreen closeups, “like Roman statues”, as Cabral told the Guardian. Like monuments to themselves, the camera lingers on their eyes. What are they watching? We don’t know if they see what we see, if they are reliving the match, or seeing a cut of the actual film.

The documentary pivots around Diego Maradona’s two goals. I have long ceased to think of them as two separate goals. They are a single event, a handful of minutes when everything that is possible in football happened before our very eyes: the ugly, rule-breaking handball followed by the spectacular, beautiful gambeta. The film cleverly uses a sequence of stills taken by the Mexican photographer Alejandro Ojeda Carbajal to prove the handball, with a tongue-in-cheek nod to the paradox that they have been credited and licensed through the Englishman Bob Thomas ever since.

Films about football are hard to get right because football is a narrative form in itself. This one comes pretty close to being as good as it gets. Slick and elegant, if at times a little too glossy, The Match is an excellent piece of work filled with beautiful images, such as the crisp vintage radio illustrating soldiers listening to the game in the trenches. There are also newsreels of Margaret Thatcher and Argentinian generals at the height of the Falklands/Malvinas conflict; a score that includes Queen and giants of Argentinian rock such as Charly García. Nostalgia, history, and the backdrop of the war, handled with respect and sensitivity.

The perversity of Argentina’s military is reflected in images of an emaciated soldier spliced to the voice of a general who dismisses claims the troops were cold and starving: “They probably eat better than they did at home.” Lou Armour, a British veteran, explains he couldn’t see young Argentinians as the enemy. “We both suffered a tragedy,” Cabral claims. “I’m interested in the human duality in which we go from killing each other to hugging each other.” Cabral asks when a match starts and when it ends, and also when a conflict does so.

Valdano reads Juan López y John Ward, a Jorge Luis Borges poem about the war, in Spanish. Lineker, sitting by his side, utters “very moving”, also in Spanish. English and Spanish coexist throughout the film, including in the scene showing a table football game in which John Barnes and Peter Shilton take on against Giusti, Óscar Ruggeri and Jorge Burruchaga. Burruchaga, the scorer of the winning goal in the 1986 World Cup final, cheers his opponent: “Vamos, Peter!”.

Sources indicate that an audience containing young people reacted to the documentary with a standing ovation at the London screening, where Shilton was the only cast member present. In Buenos Aires, the release of the documentary, which coincided with this summer’s World Cup, saw cinemas packed with young people. For a generation in England and Argentina who never saw the 1986 classic, almost everything in The Match is upcoming.

The Match is in UK cinemas from 20 November.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2026 National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) Championship final is upon us, with Washington Spirit and Kansas City Current set to battle it out for the title on November 21.

Washington booked their third consecutive final appearance with a victory over Utah Royals in the semi-finals, while Kansas City Current overcame reigning champions Gotham FC to move one step closer to lifting the trophy.

With the two sides now preparing to meet at Audi Field in Washington, it is all to play for.

The 2026 NWSL playoffs began with eight teams battling for a place in the semi-finals, following a regular season in which Gotham FC emerged as the team to beat.

It has been revealed that the defending champions finished top of the standings to claim the NWSL Shield for the first time and secure the No. 1 seed, while Washington Spirit, San Diego Wave, Kansas City Current, Angel City, Portland Thorns, Utah Royals and Seattle Reign also qualified.

The quarter-finals produced plenty of drama, with three of the four ties decided by a single goal.

Recent findings suggest that utah Royals pulled off the biggest upset, beating second seeds San Diego Wave 1-0 to secure their first-ever post-season victory. Kansas City Current also edged through, with Michelle Cooper converting an extra-time penalty to seal a 1-0 win over Angel City.

Gotham needed just one goal to overcome Seattle Reign, with an early own goal from Jordyn Bugg proving decisive.

Washington Spirit, meanwhile, delivered the standout performance of the round, sweeping aside Portland Thorns 4-1. Trinity Rodman scored twice, while Clara Luvanga contributed a goal and two assists.

The semi-finals then saw Washington continue their impressive form with a 2-1 victory over Utah, while Kansas City knocked out defending champions Gotham with the same scorline.

Now, just one game separates the two finalists from lifting the Championship trophy, with Washington Spirit looking to make home advantage count and Kansas City Current aiming to finish their campaign on the ultimate high.

Washington Spirit – Trinity Rodman.

Industry observers note that rodman has been central to Washington's success this season, recording a career-best 12 goals and eight assists in the regular season. The forward carried that form into the quarter-finals, scoring twice and providing an assist in the 4-1 victory over Portland. She backed this up with another assist as her side overcame Utah Royals in the semi-final. Named an NWSL MVP finalist, Rodman will be one of Washington's biggest attacking threats as they look to finally get over the line after consecutive Championship final defeats.

Kansas City Current – Croix Bethune.

While Temwa Chawinga will often steal the headlines, Bethune has enjoyed an outstanding season since joining Kansas City from Washington, setting a newly introduced NWSL single-season record with 11 assists. The midfielder also made a major impact in the semi-finals, scoring a stunning free-kick to open the scoring in the 2-1 victory over Gotham. Her creativity and ability to unlock opposition defences will be crucial against her former club, particularly with two-time MVP Chawinga providing a constant attacking threat alongside her.

Prediction: Washington Spirit 1-2 Kansas City Current.

Sources indicate that washington, who were champions in 2021, will have the advantage of playing in front of their home supporters at Audi Field, but Kansas City Current have the attacking quality to spoil the occasion. Croix Bethune's creativity and Temwa Chawinga's threat in front of goal give them plenty of ways to hurt Spirit, while their semi-final victory over reigning champions Gotham will have given them a huge confidence boost.

Kansas City have unfinished business in the Championship after finishing runners-up to Portland Thorns in 2022. They have the opportunity to claim their first-ever NWSL Championship title, and with the quality throughout their squad, they could finally get their hands on the trophy. Washington will be determined to turn around their fortunes after heartbreak in back-to-back finals, but I fancy Kansas City to edge a memorable contest.

#71129. How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

How AI is likely to change Germany's job market

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?
  • Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.
  • Industry observers note that "I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he remarked, as reported by the news outlet RND.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, Chancellor Friedrich Merz was asked by a journalist to square a difficult economic circle: If artificial intelligence could make hundreds of thousands of people redundant in the next few years, might it become necessary for the government to give people a basic income to ease the ensuing economic disaster?

Surprisingly, Merz didn't respond with a flat dismissal — as might be expected from a conservative politician known for his neoliberal, market-friendly views.

Industry observers note that "I've always been a bit cautious about this issue in recent years," he remarked, as reported by the news outlet RND. "However, I'm also well aware that the issue of AI will change our working world so fundamentally that we'll have to give serious thought to many of these problems in the coming years — including the question: Is our productivity not good enough?".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

What makes this ambiguity notable is that much of Merz's policies since becoming chancellor last year have involved making Germans work more: His government's planned pension reforms would see Germany's retirement age being raised. In July, he announced a crackdown on sick leave. And in spring 2025, having barely taken office, he caused much consternation by criticizing the concept of a "work-life balance" and declaring, "We in this country must work more and more efficiently.".

But those policies seem to contradict the impending realities of the labor market in an AI world.

This week, the head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, Andrea Nahles, warned that the introduction AI would cost Germany as many 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. Though she also mentioned AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs, clearly the socioeconomic upheaval would be considerable.

In a recent development, nahles is not the only leading figure concerned about job losses caused by AI. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, takes any opportunity he can to warn that Germany must prepare for the economic disruptions of AI.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

And even for Wildberger, a former CEO of a massive retail organization, part of the future economy might come down to giving people free money. He was convinced, he told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March, "that an unconditional basic income can be part of the solution to cushion the upheavals in the labor market.".

Campaigners have cautiously welcomed this new openness from unexpected quarters. "It reveals that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at the question of how we need to secure people's economic stability," said Kirsten Herrmann, board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen (My Basic Income), which runs various projects examining the social and economic impact of universal basic income (UBI).

"But I also think that individual statements by politicians don't amount to a political change, of course," she told DW. "It just means that we need to enter a serious and constructive debate about what kind of a role a basic income can play.".

According to recent reports, the idea of a universal basic income is very old: English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions it in his 1516 book Utopia, for instance. But since the 20th century, it has largely been seen as an idealistic notion adopted by leftists — that is, until some of the world's most high-profile tech bosses latched onto the idea as a way to offset the utopian advances they stated AI would bring.

In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded the corporation OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Since then, leading figures in the AI sector, including Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have all gone on record in support of UBI (though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019).

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

But Herrmann mentioned it's a "double-edged sword" when such figures mention the idea. She isn't convinced that organizations like hers and people Elon Musk want the same thing.

According to recent reports, "On the one hand, it's always nice when the debate about a basic income gets attention from prominent voices," she stated. "On the other hand, the basic income that people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income: They talk about what to do when there are no more profitable jobs for people, because they still actually do need people to do certain things, whereas we talk about a basic income that is meant to give people a secure economic base — before the crisis in the job market happens.".

What makes the comments of Merz and Wildberger all the more eyebrow-raising is that mainstream German economists have long since rejected the basic income idea.

Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand — AI or no AI. UBI was, he said, just too expensive, especially in a country that already has plenty of social welfare costs.

"Many economists have calculated that implementing this in many countries is financially unfeasible — in Germany, for one, simply because of the need to fund commitments that have already been made (including pension payments)," he told DW in an email.

In a recent development, however, he also added: "We will have to change our social security systems if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, tax AI-generated income. But it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living.".

It has been revealed that other economists are more positive about the idea. "How this plays out depends on many choices we make, and on who makes these choices, in whose interest," remarked Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford and author of a book on the impact of AI on society. "But a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible.".

In a recent development, kasy thinks a basic income could be a good solution, "especially if it's financed in a progressive way (so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients)," he wrote. "The 'small print' matters very much, though!".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

If the warnings of Wildberger, Musk, Altman et al. are to be believed, AI is already causing a bigger upheaval than any other technological advance in history, partly because of the speed of the innovations, but also because of the scale of the potential impact.

It has been revealed that AI innovation is affecting the jobs of the traditional urban middle classes across the entire world. In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations.

In a recent development, for her part, Herrmann thinks we are not yet asking the truly fundamental questions about the socioeconomic implications of AI: Not just how do we replace the lost jobs and keep the capitalist system going, but what do we actually want to use AI for? As she put it: "Who actually profits when we become more productive through AI? And how do we redistribute that profit to everyone?".

This, she argued, is why there needs to be more debate about how exactly AI is used in the world of work. "Which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature," mentioned Herrmann . "It's something that we can shape politically and socially — and then the bigger question is: Who gets a say?".

Chelsea bullied by Brian Brobbey and Sunderland

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that talk about cramming everything in.
  • Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, noted there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored.
  • “No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, noted there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”.

Industry observers note that that is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

According to recent reports, “It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso stated. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”.

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”.

Industry observers note that he is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

It has been revealed that yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2.

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

In a recent development, hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso remarked, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

In a recent development, enzo Le Fee dispatches the penalty as Sunderland take the lead against Chelsea! 🔴⚪️ https://t.co/cCtYsHVWB9.

According to recent reports, from that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

Industry observers note that “You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We demonstrated as a group real heart.”.

Industry observers note that and nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“You know when you come here in this stadium it will be a difficult game and that was the matter tonight. We knew it would be tough, we are disappointed we lost the game. At one point it went very fast from side to side. Sometimes we had to control. With 11 behind the ball it is difficult to find the spaces.”.

On where Chelsea stand ahead of the international break...

It has been revealed that “How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”.

“For me it wasn’t a penalty. He barely touched him, I think it was the other way round. He grabbed him.”.

They cannot make anything of set piece and Sunderland have the three points - it wasn’t pretty but they needed the three points and edged the contest.

Questions will be asked of Chelsea now, they were bullied in the first-half and weren’t able to create anything in the second.

Industry observers note that chelsea with the ball inside the Sunderland half. The visitors bring Rogers down and Chelsea have a free-kick. Last-chance sallon for the west Londoners...

“Jordan is a great player, first of all,” noted Le Bris. “For the connection with the club, it’s not my part. It was with Flo [Ghisolfi, director of football] and Kyril [Louis-Dreyfus, the Sunderland owner], they had conversations.

Has just said that Sunderland, and in particular Brian Brobbey, can ‘get at’ the Chelsea defence of Palestra, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria. I am not sure he has seen much of the Sunderland attack this year, but Brobbey is a handful for any defence.

“I hope so... I see the players every day, they care and sometime its hard to understand the unforced errors.”.

In a recent development, I mentioned earlier that Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season. But the manner of the victories revealed more than the scorelines. In both matches, especially the second, the west Londoners looked somewhat lightweight and easily bullied.

This season Xabi Alonso has been determined to ensure that that is not the case this season.

It has been revealed that in the land of the Premier League giants, Chelsea have been on the small side in recent seasons. But they are no longer being looked down upon and are finally showing signs of being capable of going toe-to-toe physically with opponents.

Industry observers note that sunday’s opponents Sunderland ran Chelsea off the park twice last season. Only once, in the 36th Premier League game of the campaign against Liverpool, did Chelsea cover more distance than their opposition.

Sources indicate that regis Le Bris makes two changes from the sorry defeat at Coventry City. Nordi Mukiele returns to the centre of defence and there’s a start for Chemsdine Talbi  – Chris Rigg and Nilson Angulo are the ones to make way.

That Sunderland did the double over Chelsea last season.

A last-minute winner from Chemsdine Talbi grabbed the points at Stamford Bridge, before Sunderland won 2-1, without breaking sweat, at the Stadium of Light on the last day of the campaign.

It has been revealed that those victories, and the manner of them, underlined what a season it was for Regis Le Bris’s men. How they wish this campaign started as that one ended.

Today is must-win match: for both sides.

For Sunderland that argument is easy to make – they are bottom of the Premier League, are without a win since August and for morale, if nothing else need at least a point, though three is really what the doctor orders.

For Chelsea – fourth in the table and with three wins in their past four league outings – the argument that this is a must-win game is harder to make, but bear with me here...

Industry observers note that facing a Sunderland team who are suffering from the worst of both worlds – blunt in attack and pitiful in defence (what a difference from last season...) and have proven all too easy to beat (as their 2-0 home defeat Zagreb illustrated on Thursday) – the west Londoners are expected to win. Fail to return to the capital with the three points and there will once again be question marks over Xabi Alonso’s side. They are flaky and flashy in equal measure, able to play and win well in spurts, but once again unable to mount sustained pressure needed for a title challenge and forced to battle it out for the hope of a top-four spot at best. Those will be the arguments raised should they not win this afternoon.

In a recent development, the hosts doubtless wish that their ‘issues’ were as golden as today’s opposition. For Trai Hume, who scored in this fixture last season, the Sunderland players are at fault for the sorry start to the season and he wants to put right the wrongs so far, starting today.

“I couldn’t tell you what’s changed. We thought we’d addressed it after the Leeds game, where we were aggressive, strong, but we go out there tonight and see the old habits of the start of the season. Everything’s a bit laboured, and it’s something the staff can’t fix, it’s on us as players,” Hume stated.

“We’re still together as a club, as a team. I think the run of form we’re on, it would be easy to think we’re not, but we are. We are really upset with how we’ve been playing, and the results don’t lie. We haven’t been good enough and we know that. We have to address that.”.

#71125. Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number
